subject: chemistry
topic: Qualitative analysis (tests for ions and gases)

kept.q: A student bubbles a colourless gas through freshly prepared lime water (calcium hydroxide solution) in a test tube. The lime water turns milky (cloudy white). Which gas was most likely passed through the lime water?
options: Oxygen
Carbon(IV) oxide
Hydrogen
Nitrogen
kept.explanation: Carbon(IV) oxide (CO2) reacts with lime water to form a white insoluble precipitate of calcium trioxocarbonate(IV), CaCO3, which makes the solution milky. This is the standard confirmatory test for CO2 gas.
kept.pidgin: CO2 gas dey turn lime water milky because e dey form white CaCO3 precipitate wey no dey dissolve. Na the standard test wey dem dey use check CO2 for lab.

kept.q: A gas with a choking smell is produced when ammonium chloride is heated with sodium hydroxide solution. When a piece of moist red litmus paper is held near the mouth of the test tube, the paper turns blue. Which gas is being tested for?
options: Chlorine gas
Sulphur(IV) oxide
Ammonia gas
Hydrogen chloride gas
kept.explanation: Ammonia gas (NH3) is alkaline and has a sharp, choking smell; it turns moist red litmus paper blue. This is the classic test used to confirm the presence of ammonium ions in a compound.
kept.pidgin: Ammonia gas get strong choking smell and e be alkaline, so e dey turn wet red litmus paper to blue. Na so dem dey test for ammonium ion for compound.

kept.q: Chidinma was given two separate solutions labelled X and Y. Solution X contains iron(II) sulphate while solution Y contains iron(III) chloride, but the labels have fallen off. She adds sodium hydroxide solution dropwise to each. Which observation would correctly help her identify solution Y?
options: A dirty green precipitate forms, insoluble in excess NaOH
A reddish-brown precipitate forms, insoluble in excess NaOH
A white precipitate forms, which dissolves in excess NaOH
No precipitate forms at all
kept.explanation: Iron(III) ions (Fe3+) react with sodium hydroxide to give a reddish-brown precipitate of Fe(OH)3, which does not dissolve in excess NaOH. Iron(II) ions instead give a dirty green precipitate of Fe(OH)2, so the reddish-brown colour identifies solution Y as iron(III) chloride.
kept.pidgin: Fe3+ ion dey react with NaOH give reddish-brown precipitate (Fe(OH)3) wey no dey dissolve for excess NaOH. Fe2+ go give dirty green precipitate instead, so reddish-brown na im go show say na Fe3+ dey solution Y.

kept.q: A colourless salt solution is suspected to contain chloride ions. Dilute trioxonitrate(V) acid (dilute nitric acid) is added, followed by silver trioxonitrate(V) solution. A white precipitate forms. To confirm that the precipitate is indeed silver chloride and not another silver salt, what should be done next?
options: Heat the precipitate strongly until it melts
Add excess dilute hydrochloric acid and observe if the precipitate increases
Add dilute (aqueous) ammonia solution and observe if the precipitate dissolves
Add excess sodium chloride solution and observe the colour change
kept.explanation: Silver chloride is a white precipitate that readily dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia solution to form a soluble complex, [Ag(NH3)2]+. This solubility in dilute ammonia distinguishes it from silver carbonate or silver sulphate precipitates, confirming the presence of chloride ions.
kept.pidgin: Silver chloride na white precipitate wey dey dissolve for dilute ammonia solution because e dey form soluble complex. Dis solubility test dey confirm say na chloride ion dey inside, e dey different from other silver salts.

kept.q: Two white solid salts, P and Q, are each suspected to be either sodium trioxosulphate(IV) (sodium sulphite) or sodium tetraoxosulphate(VI) (sodium sulphate). Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to each solid separately. Salt P produces a colourless gas with a sharp, choking smell that turns acidified potassium heptaoxomanganate(VII) (potassium permanganate) solution from purple to colourless. Salt Q shows no visible reaction. What can be correctly concluded?
options: P is sodium sulphate and Q is sodium sulphite
P is sodium sulphite and Q is sodium sulphate
Both P and Q are sodium sulphate
Both P and Q are sodium sulphite
kept.explanation: Sulphite ions (SO3^2-) react with dilute HCl to release sulphur(IV) oxide gas (SO2), which has a choking smell and decolourises acidified potassium permanganate due to its reducing property. Sulphate ions (SO4^2-) do not react with dilute HCl because they are already fully oxidised, so Q showing no reaction must be sodium sulphate.
kept.pidgin: Sulphite ion (SO3^2-) dey react with dilute HCl produce SO2 gas wey get choking smell and e dey decolourise potassium permanganate because e be reducing agent. Sulphate ion no dey react with dilute HCl at all, so Q wey no show reaction na sodium sulphate.

kept.q: Two colourless salt solutions, R and S, are each known to contain either zinc(II) ions or lead(II) ions. When potassium iodide solution is added dropwise to each, solution R produces a bright yellow precipitate while solution S shows no visible precipitate. Based on this observation, which statement is correct?
options: R contains Zn2+ and S contains Pb2+
R contains Pb2+ and S contains Zn2+
Both R and S contain Pb2+
Both R and S contain Zn2+
kept.explanation: Lead(II) ions react with potassium iodide to form a characteristic bright yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide, PbI2. Zinc(II) ions do not form a precipitate with potassium iodide since zinc iodide is soluble, so solution S with no precipitate must contain Zn2+.
kept.pidgin: Lead(II) ion dey react with potassium iodide give bright yellow precipitate (PbI2). Zinc ion no dey form any precipitate with potassium iodide because zinc iodide dey soluble, so S wey no get precipitate na Zn2+ dey inside.
